rows.why: Item 10 asks whether expiry runs from creation time. Its pick sets expiresAt to the creation time plus a fixed 14 days, which gives 2026-03-15T09:00:00Z as the scenario expects. No item covers re-drawing a code that collides with an existing one.
No item asks what a successful redemption grants or records: access to only that task, plus who used the code and when.
Item 4 asks how a typed code is matched by case, whitespace and dashes. Its pick removes whitespace and '-' and uppercases the input, so lowercase, spaced and dashed input all match the same code.
Item 1 asks whether a code works at the exact 14-day instant. Its pick treats now >= createdAt + 14 days as expired, so the code works at 08:59:59.999Z and fails with 'expired' at 09:00:00Z.

No item asks what happens when someone else redeems a used code (reason 'used'). No item asks whether the same person can redeem their own used code again and succeed. Item 2 is about redeeming a different code for a task you already have, which S7 covers, so it does not settle this.

Item 5 asks what redeeming an unknown code reports. Its pick returns { ok: false, reason: 'unknown' }, as the scenario expects. Item 6 touches the 'used code cannot be revoked' clause, and its pick of throwing is consistent with that, but item 5 is the closer match to the scenario's main question.
Item 2 asks what happens when someone redeems a code for a task they already have access to. Its pick returns reason 'already has access' and leaves the code unused, exactly as the scenario expects.

Item 9 asks how simultaneous operations on the same registry are handled. Its pick runs operations one at a time within the instance, so the second redemption sees the code as used: exactly one succeeds and the other fails with 'used'.

Item 3 asks which state to report for a code that is both used and past expiry. Its pick checks used before expired, so a used code still shows 'used' after its expiry time, as the scenario requires. Item 11 is only about listing order and the empty case, so it fits less closely.
